newsitem.title: USA: Babbitt holds wry "party" for 1872 mining law.
newsitem.headline: Babbitt holds wry "party" for 1872 mining law.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt staged a mock "birthday party" Monday for a 125-year-old mining law he says is costing the U.S. government hundreds of millions of dollars per year.

The 1872 Mining Law, which allows miners to claim ownership of public land for as little at $2.50 an acre, has allowed for the sale of 5,138 acres of land holding $15 billion in minerals in the past three years for just $23,601, Babbit and other critics say.

In a wry "birthday party" for the law in the Interior Department's New Deal-era auditorium, Babbitt signed over 248 acres of federal land near Elko, Nevada, for $620. Gold underneath the land might be worth $110 million, he said.
"This is probably my 125th news conference on the Mining Law of 1872. I acknowledge it's getting old," Babbitt said.

He was joined in decrying the law by Senator Dale Bumpers, Arkansas Democrat, sponsor of legislation to levy a royalty and an assessment to pay for land reclamation, and two consumer groups. One was a fiscal watchdog and the other advocated reform of laws governing mining of hard-rock minerals, such as gold, silver and copper, on federal land.

The National Mining Assocation, a trade group, faulted Babbitt for "publicity stunts" and said it agreed to the need for reform of the law. Its changes would produce about $157 million a year in revenues.

"We believe the gap between what Congress has approved and the administration seeks has been narrowed and that the timely enactment of fair, balanced mining law reform is within grasp," NMA said in a statement.

Bumpers' package, and a companion House package, would generate $1.5 billion in five years, sponsors said when they filed the bills in mid-February. They lay moribund since. The bills fulfilled a promise the White House made in calling from reform this year.
NMA said the U.S. mining industry produced $1 billion in taxes each year. Mineral reserves are worth nothing until the expensive process of mining, its advocates said.
